title: Data Generation : Mepolizumab case study (recurrent event endpoint)
text: initializing RecurrentEventTargetData object, start computing rate arm based drift arm (default, drift control arms, control drift, 0) compute standard deviation logRR. Importantly, want able introduce change source study control rate compute corresponding logRR. negative binomial distribution, mean μ\mu variance σ2\sigma^2 given : μ=r(1−p)p \mu = \frac{r(1-p)}{p} σ2=r(1−p)p2 \sigma^2 = \frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}  rr number successes pp probability success trial. standard error mean : SE=σn=r(1−p)p2n=r(1−p)np2 \text{SE} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}}}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{r(1-p)}{n p^2}} negative binomial distribution can parameterized different ways, common parameterization involves mean μ\mu dispersion parameter kk. mean μ\mu expected number failures achieving kk successes. parameterization, mean μ\mu variance σ2\sigma^2 related follows: μ=k(1−p)p \mu = \frac{k(1-p)}{p} variance σ2\sigma^2 given : σ2=k(1−p)p2 \sigma^2 = \frac{k(1-p)}{p^2} can express variance terms μ\mu kk. mean equation, can solve pp: p=kk+μ p = \frac{k}{k + \mu} Substituting pp back variance equation: σ2=k(1−kk+μ)(kk+μ)2 \sigma^2 = \frac{k \left(1 - \frac{k}{k + \mu}\right)}{\left(\frac{k}{k + \mu}\right)^2} σ2=μ(k+μ)k \sigma^2 = \frac{\mu (k + \mu)}{k} Therefore, standard deviation negative binomial distribution mean μ\mu size parameter kk : σ=μ+μ2k \sigma = \sqrt{\mu + \frac{\mu^2}{k}} Moreover, using delta method, standard error log event rate ratio approximated : SE(log(λtλc))≈(SE(λt)λt)2+(SE(λc)λc)2 \text{SE}\left(\log\left(\frac{\lambda_t}{\lambda_c}\right)\right) \approx \sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{SE}(\lambda_t)}{\lambda_t}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\text{SE}(\lambda_c)}{\lambda_c}\right)^2} : SE(log(λtλc))≈1nt⋅(μt+μt2kμt)2+1nc⋅(μc+μc2kμc)2 \text{SE}\left(\log\left(\frac{\lambda_t}{\lambda_c}\right)\right) \approx \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_t} \cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{\mu_t + \frac{\mu_t^2}{k}}}{\mu_t}\right)^2 + \frac{1}{n_c} \cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{\mu_c + \frac{\mu_c^2}{k}}}{\mu_c}\right)^2} compared SE Ortega et al (2014), 0.130. compare result SE obtained simulation: average compared treatment effect Ortega et al (2014), -0.69.

source_data <- SourceData$new(case_study_config)  drift <- 0.4 target_sample_size_per_arm <- 225 target_data <- TargetDataFactory$new() target_data <- target_data$create(source_data = source_data, case_study_config = case_study_config, target_sample_size_per_arm = target_sample_size_per_arm, treatment_drift = drift, summary_measure_likelihood = source_data$summary_measure_likelihood) read_function_code(rate_from_drift_logRR) ## rate_from_drift_logRR <- function (arm_drift, source_rate)  ## { ##     return(source_rate * exp(arm_drift)) ## } control_drift <- 0 treatment_drift <- drift + control_drift  target_data$control_rate <- rate_from_drift_logRR(control_drift, source_data$control_rate) target_data$treatment_rate <- rate_from_drift_logRR(treatment_drift, source_data$treatment_rate)  target_data$treatment_effect <- target_data$drift + source_data$treatment_effect_estimate mu_treatment <- target_data$treatment_rate # Mean of the first rate mu_control <- target_data$control_rate # Mean of the second rate k_treatment <- 0.8 # Size parameter of the first negative binomial distribution k_control <- 0.8 # Size parameter of the second negative binomial distribution n_treatment <- target_data$sample_size_per_arm # Sample size for the first rate n_control <- target_data$sample_size_per_arm # Sample size for the second rate  # Compute the standard deviations for the negative binomial distributions sigma_treatment <- sqrt(mu_treatment + (mu_treatment^2 / k_treatment)) sigma_control <- sqrt(mu_control + (mu_control^2 / k_control))  # Compute the standard errors of the rates SE_R_treatment <- sigma_treatment / sqrt(n_treatment) SE_R_control <- sigma_control / sqrt(n_control)  target_data$standard_deviation <- sqrt(target_data$sample_size_per_arm) * sqrt((SE_R_treatment / mu_treatment)^   2 + (SE_R_control / mu_control)^2)  # Compute the SE of the log rate ratio SE_log_rate_ratio <- target_data$standard_deviation / sqrt(target_data$sample_size_per_arm)   cat("The standard error of the log rate ratio is:", SE_log_rate_ratio, "
") ## The standard error of the log rate ratio is: 0.1307278 n_replicates <- 10000 log_rate_ratios <- numeric(n_replicates) se_log_rate_ratios <- numeric(n_replicates) for (i in 1:n_replicates) {   # Generate the patient-level data by sampling from negative binomial distributions   source_data_control <- rnbinom(n_control, size = 1 / k_control, mu = mu_control)   source_data_treatment <- rnbinom(n_treatment, size = 1 / k_treatment, mu = mu_treatment)   treatment <- negative_binomial_regression(source_data_treatment)   control <- negative_binomial_regression(source_data_control)   log_rate_ratio <- log(treatment$rate_estimate) - log(control$rate_estimate)    # Calculate the SE of the log rate ratio   log_rate_ratios[i] <- log_rate_ratio   se_log_rate_ratios[i] <- sqrt(treatment$se_log_rate^2 + control$se_log_rate^2) }  cat("The standard error on the log rate ratio is:", sd(log_rate_ratios), "

text: location commensurate power prior given Hobbs et al (2011): π(θT,γ,τ|𝐃𝐒)=∫π(θT|θS,τ)ℒ(θS|𝐃S)γπ0(θS)∫ℒ(θS|𝐃S)γπ0(θS)dθSdθS×p(γ|τ)p(τ) \pi(\theta_T, \gamma, \tau| \mathbf{D_S})   = \int \pi(\theta_T|\theta_S, \tau) \frac{\mathcal{L}(\theta_S | \mathbf{D}_S)^\gamma \pi_0(\theta_S)}{\int \mathcal{L}(\theta_S | \mathbf{D}_S)^\gamma \pi_0(\theta_S) d\theta_S}d\theta_S \times p(\gamma|\tau) p(\tau) π0(θS)\pi_0(\theta_S) initial prior θS\theta_S. Note , compared equation (4) Hobbs et al (2011), prior differs slightly. Indeed, paper, prior π0(θS)\pi_0(\theta_S) omitted, dθSd\theta_S misplaced. Hobbs et al (2011) chose following distributions: θT|θS,τ∼𝒩(θS,1τ), \theta_T|\theta_S, \tau \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\theta_S, \frac{1}{\tau}\right), γ|τ∼Beta(g(τ),1), \gamma | \tau \sim Beta(g(\tau),1), g(τ)g(\tau) positive function τ\tau small τ\tau closed zero large large values τ\tau. evidence commensurability weak, τ\tau forced toward zero, increasing variance commensurate prior θT\theta_T. amount borrowing can adapted two ways: specification p(γ|τ)p(\gamma|\tau), p(τ)p(\tau).

title: Commensurate Power Prior
text: Hobbs et al (2011) show , Gaussian likelihood case (equation 9): p(θT∣𝐃S,𝐃T,γ,τ,σ2)∝N(θT|γNSτσ2θ̂S+NTuθ̂TγNSτσ2+NTu,uσ2γNSτσ2+NTu) p\left(\theta_T \mid \mathbf{D}_{S}, \mathbf{D}_T, \gamma, \tau, \sigma^2\right) \propto N\left(\theta_T \left\lvert\, \frac{\gamma N_S \tau \sigma^2 \hat{\theta}_S+N_T u \hat{\theta}_T}{\gamma N_S \tau \sigma^2+N_T u}\right., \frac{u \sigma^2}{\gamma N_S \tau \sigma^2+ N_T u}\right) u=γNS+σ̂S2τu=\gamma N_S+\hat{\sigma}_S^2 \tau, p(γ,τ∣𝐃S,𝐃T,σ2)∝N(θ̂T−θ̂S∣0,σ2NT+1τ+σ̂S2γNS)×Beta⁡(γ∣g(τ),1)×π(τ). \begin{aligned} p\left(\gamma, \tau \mid \mathbf{D}_S, \mathbf{D}_T, \sigma^2\right) \propto & N\left(\hat{\theta}_T-\hat{\theta}_S \mid 0, \frac{\sigma^2}{N_T}+\frac{1}{\tau}+\frac{\hat{\sigma}_S^2}{\gamma N_S}\right) \\ & \times \operatorname{Beta}\left(\gamma \mid g(\tau), 1\right) \times \pi(\tau) . \end{aligned}

text: pooling, prior distribution θT\theta_T given : p(θT)=𝒩(θT|θ̂S,σS2/NS) p(\theta_T) = \mathcal{N}(\theta_T | \hat{\theta}_S, \sigma^2_S/N_S) observe NTN_T data points sample mean θ̂T\hat{\theta}_T known variance σT2\sigma^2_T. implies likelihood given : p(θ̂T|θT)=𝒩(θ̂T|θT,σT2/NT) p(\hat{\theta}_T | \theta_T) = \mathcal{N}(\hat{\theta}_T | \theta_T, \sigma^2_T/N_T) Since prior likelihood Gaussian distributions, posterior also Gaussian distribution. posterior distribution p(θT|θ̂T)p(\theta_T | \hat{\theta}_T) : θT|θ̂T∼𝒩(μpost,σpost2) \theta_T | \hat{\theta}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{\text{post}}, \sigma^2_{\text{post}}) Posterior Mean: μpost=σpost2(θ̂SNSσS2+θ̂TNTσT2) \mu_{\text{post}} = \sigma_{\text{post}}^2 \left( \frac{\hat{\theta}_S N_S}{\sigma^2_S} + \frac{\hat{\theta}_T N_T}{\sigma^2_T} \right) Posterior Variance: σpost2=(NSσS2+NTσT2)−1 \sigma_{\text{post}}^2 = \left( \frac{N_S}{\sigma^2_S} + \frac{N_T}{\sigma^2_T} \right)^{-1} Thus, posterior distribution p(θT|θ̂T)p(\theta_T | \hat{\theta}_T) : θT|θ̂T∼N((NSσS2+NTσT2)−1(θ̂SNSσS2+θ̂TNTσT2),(NSσS2+NTσT2)−1) \theta_T | \hat{\theta}_T \sim N\left( \left( \frac{N_S}{\sigma^2_S} + \frac{N_T}{\sigma^2_T} \right)^{-1} \left( \frac{\hat{\theta}_S N_S}{\sigma^2_S} + \frac{\hat{\theta}_T N_T}{\sigma^2_T} \right), \left( \frac{N_S}{\sigma^2_S} + \frac{N_T}{\sigma^2_T} \right)^{-1} \right) limit σT\sigma_T goes infinity: σpost2→σS2NS \sigma_{\text{post}}^2 \rightarrow \frac{\sigma^2_S}{N_S} μpost→θ̂S \mu_{\text{post}} \rightarrow \hat{\theta}_S , target study data discarded likelihood becomes flat, posterior prior. Pooling data equivalent defining Gaussian prior mean standard deviation corresponding treatment effect estimate standard error treatment effect source study.

code: # Define a vector of treatment effect values to loop over treatment_effect_values <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.1)  # Initialize an empty list to store dataframes data_list <- list()  # Loop over treatment effect values for (treatment_effect in treatment_effect_values) {   # Calculate the drift   drift <- treatment_effect - source_data$treatment_effect_estimate    # Create target data   target_data <- TargetDataFactory$new()   target_data <- target_data$create(     source_data = source_data,     case_study_config = case_study_config,     target_sample_size_per_arm = target_sample_size_per_arm,     treatment_drift = drift,     summary_measure_likelihood = source_data$summary_measure_likelihood   )    # Generate samples   samples <- target_data$generate(1000)    # Create a dataframe from the samples   data <- data.frame(     treatment_effect = treatment_effect,     treatment_effect_estimate = samples$treatment_effect_estimate,     treatment_effect_standard_error = samples$treatment_effect_standard_error   )    # Append the dataframe to the list   data_list[[length(data_list) + 1]] <- data }  # Combine all dataframes into a single dataframe combined_data <- dplyr::bind_rows(data_list)  ggplot(combined_data, aes(x = treatment_effect_estimate, y = treatment_effect_standard_error)) +   geom_point(color = "blue") +   ggplot2::labs(     title = "Standard Error vs. Treatment Effect Estimate",     x = "Treatment Effect Estimate",     y = "Standard Error"   ) +   theme_minimal()

code: source_data <- ObservedSourceData$new(case_study_config) target_data <- ObservedTargetData$new(treatment_effect_estimate = case_study_config$target$treatment_effect, treatment_effect_standard_error = case_study_config$target$standard_error, target_sample_size_per_arm = as.integer(case_study_config$target$total / 2), summary_measure_likelihood = case_study_config$summary_measure_likelihood)

title: Replication of the Belimumab case study
text: parameter, instantiate model, perform Bayesian inference compute posterior mean credible interval. model instantiation relies -called factory design pattern increased ease use flexibility.
code: point_est <- numeric(Nw) credible_intervals <- matrix(NA, 2, Nw) confidence_level <- 0.95 lower_quantile <- (1 - confidence_level) / 2 upper_quantile <- 1 - lower_quantile  posterior_w <- numeric(Nw) for (i in seq_along(w_range)) {   method_parameters$prior_weight <- w_range[i]    model <- Model$new()   model <- model$create(     case_study_config = case_study_config,     method = method,     method_parameters = method_parameters,     source_data = source_data   )    # Perform Bayesian inference based on observed target data.   model$inference(target_data = target_data)    # Convert the estimates back to the natural scale   point_est[i] <- exp(model$posterior_mean())    # To estimate the credible intervals, we sample from the posterior distribution   posterior_samples <- exp(model$sample_posterior(10000))   credible_intervals[, i] <- quantile(posterior_samples, probs = c(lower_quantile, upper_quantile))   posterior_w[i] <- model$wpost }

text: Create source_data instance, information source data stored Set observed target data (paediatrics population) Robust mixture prior =w×Normal⁡(madult ,vadult )+(1−w)×Normal⁡(mweak ,vweak ) \text { Robust mixture prior }  =w \times \operatorname{Normal}\left(m_{\text {adult }}, v_{\text {adult }}\right)+(1-w) \times \operatorname{Normal}\left(m_{\text {weak }}, v_{\text {weak }}\right) Robust mixture prior =w×Normal⁡(−0.694,0.017)+(1−w)×Normal⁡(0,12.4) \text { Robust mixture prior }=w \times \operatorname{Normal}(-0.694,0.017)+(1-w) \times \operatorname{Normal}(0,12.4) Note , moment, code allow specifying different sample sizes arms target study.

code: n_samples_posterior <- 10000000  point_est <- numeric(Nw) credible_intervals <- matrix(NA, 2, Nw) confidence_level <- 0.95 lower_quantile <- (1 - confidence_level) / 2 upper_quantile <- 1 - lower_quantile  posterior_w <- numeric(Nw)  for (i in seq_along(w_range)) {   method_parameters$prior_weight <- w_range[i]    model <- Model$new()   model <- model$create(     case_study_config = case_study_config,     method = method,     method_parameters = method_parameters,     source_data = source_data   )    model$vague_prior_variance <- n_paediatrics * target_data$sample$treatment_effect_standard_error^2 # Following Best et al, 2021.    # Perform Bayesian inference based on observed target data.   model$inference(target_data = target_data)    # Convert the estimates back to the natural scale   point_est[i] <- exp(model$posterior_mean())    # To estimate the credible intervals, we sample from the posterior distribution   posterior_samples <- exp(model$sample_posterior(n_samples_posterior))   credible_intervals[, i] <- quantile(posterior_samples, probs = c(lower_quantile, upper_quantile))   posterior_w[i] <- model$wpost }
